game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value now is 0.5 × 6 + 0.5 × 3 = 4.5: half the time the coin is double-headed and the contract settles at 6, otherwise it averages 3 heads.

- **Ask (5.6):** I set the ask 1.1 above fair value because informed traders often know the value is 6. At 5.6, I lose only 0.4 per unit when that happens.
- **Bid (3.4):** I set the bid 1.1 below fair value, which leaves room against informed sellers who know the value is 3 or less. Those cases are about 33% of the time.
- **Noise traders:** Their valuations spread with standard deviation 2.6, so they should still trade fairly often at these prices.

{"bid": 3.4, "ask": 5.6}

After the first trade, my estimate of the settlement value is about 4.9.

- **Before any trades:** a fair coin gives an average of 3 heads and the always-heads coin gives 6. Each coin is equally likely, so the starting value was 4.5.
- **What the buy tells me:** a buyer at 5.6 is either informed or a noise trader who happened to value it high. An informed buyer at 5.6 means the value is 6, which almost always means the always-heads coin. Weighing both cases, the chance of the always-heads coin rises to about 0.63. That gives a value of about 0.63 × 6 + 0.37 × 3 ≈ 4.9.
- **Ask at 5.9:** the value can't exceed 6, so an informed buyer at 5.9 costs me at most 0.1 per unit. I'm already short 1, so a high ask also protects that position.
- **Bid at 3.9:** about one point below my value estimate. That covers the risk of trading against an informed seller.

{"bid": 3.9, "ask": 5.9}

Two heads in two flips makes the biased coin much more likely. The chance the coin is the always-heads one is now (0.5·1) / (0.5·1 + 0.5·0.25) = **0.8**. That gives a fair value of 2 + 4·(0.8·1 + 0.2·0.5) = **5.6**.

**Ask at 6.0:**
- If the coin is biased, settlement is exactly 6. An informed trader only buys if its value is strictly above my ask, so it won't buy at 6.0. I can't lose on that case.
- Noise traders value the contract at 5.6 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6. About 44% of them value it above 6.0, and each such sale earns me about 0.4 over fair value.

**Bid at 4.5:**
- Noise traders sell below 4.5 about 34% of the time. Each such buy earns me about 1.1 over fair value.
- The risk is an informed trader when the coin is fair, where settlement averages 4. That is a small part of the flow, and the wide edge against noise traders covers it.

I'm ignoring the small information in the stage-1 trades.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 6.0}

Fair value is about 5.6, from the posterior on the coin given the two revealed heads.

**Posterior on the coin.** Flips 1 and 2 were both heads.
- Under the fair coin, two heads has likelihood 0.25.
- Under the always-heads coin, the likelihood is 1.
- So P(always-heads) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.125) = 0.8.

**Fair value.**
- Two heads are already in.
- The 4 remaining flips give an expected 0.8 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 = 3.6 more heads.
- Fair value ≈ 2 + 3.6 = 5.6.
- I ignored the no-trade at quote 3 (bid 4.5, ask 6) as only weak information.

**Ask.** Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.81: 0.8 from the always-heads coin plus 0.2 × 1/16 from the fair coin. An informed trader holding 6 buys only if my ask is below 6. An ask of 6.0 therefore avoids most adverse selection. Noise traders still buy it with probability about 0.44 (P(5.6 + noise > 6)), at a price above fair value.

**Bid.** At 4.6, informed traders sell only if the settlement value is 4 or less. That needs the fair coin plus at most 2 heads in the last 4 flips, so probability 0.2 × 11/16 ≈ 0.14. Noise traders sell with probability about 0.35, buying at about 1 below fair value.

{"bid": 4.6, "ask": 6.0}

With four heads out of four flips, the biased coin is very likely and the contract should settle at about 5.94.

**Fair value**
- Four straight heads make the coin almost certainly the always-heads one. P(always-heads coin) = 1 / (1 + 1/16) = 16/17.
- Flips 5 and 6 add 2 expected heads with that coin and 1 with the fair coin.
- Expected settlement = 4 + (16/17)·2 + (1/17)·1 ≈ 5.94.
- Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.956, 5 with about 0.029 and 4 with about 0.015.

**Informed traders**
- An informed trader buys only if the true value is above my ask. The value is at most 6, so an ask of 6.0 or higher cannot lose to them on that side.
- They sell only if the value is below my bid. With a bid of 4.0 that is nearly impossible.

**Noise traders**
Their valuations are about 5.94 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6. Expected gain from a noise trade is roughly P(trade) × edge:

| Side | Price | P(trade) | Edge | Expected gain |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bid | 5.0 | 0.36 | 0.94 | 0.34 |
| Bid | 4.5 | 0.29 | 1.44 | 0.42 |
| Bid | **4.0** | 0.23 | 1.94 | **0.45** |
| Bid | 3.5 | 0.17 | 2.44 | 0.42 |
| Ask | 6.5 | 0.33 | 0.56 | 0.18 |
| Ask | **7.0** | 0.23 | 1.06 | **0.24** |
| Ask | 7.5 | 0.14 | 1.56 | 0.22 |
| Ask | 8.0 | 0.07 | 2.06 | 0.15 |

The best prices are a bid of 4.0 and an ask of 7.0. My position of -1 leaves room to trade on either side.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.0}

Four heads have been revealed, so the settlement is at least 4. I quote a bid of 4.0 and an ask of 6.0.

**Posterior on the coin.** Before any flips, each coin has probability 1/2.
- The chance of four heads is 1/16 for the fair coin and 1 for the always-heads coin.
- So P(always-heads) = 16/17 and P(fair) = 1/17.
- The trade at quote 5 was a sale to me at 4. An informed trader never sells at 4 because the value is at least 4, so that trader was noise and the trade tells us nothing.

**Settlement value.**
- Expected value = 4 + (16/17 × 2) + (1/17 × 1) ≈ 5.94.
- The value is 6 with probability about 0.956, 5 with about 0.029, and 4 with about 0.015.

**Ask at 6.0.** The value can never exceed 6, so an informed trader never buys at 6.0. A noise trader buys about half the time, giving me a small gain each time.

**Bid at 4.0.** The expected profit per quote is roughly 0.8 × P(noise sells) × (5.94 − bid), less a small informed loss:
- Bid 5.0: about 0.27
- Bid 4.5: about 0.33
- Bid 4.0: about 0.36

An informed trader never sells at 4.0, since the value is at least 4.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 6.0}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value is 4.5. With probability ½ the coin is the always-heads coin, so the contract settles at 6. Otherwise it is a fair coin and the contract settles at Binomial(6, 0.5), with mean 3.

Informed traders buy whenever the value is 6. If my ask is just under 6, they make almost nothing from it. Noise traders who buy up there pay well above fair value.

On the bid side, informed traders sell when the value is low. Setting the bid near 3 limits that loss. Noise sellers at that level give me about 1.5 of edge per trade.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.9}

The sell at 3 lowers my estimate of the value to about 3.6, from 4.5 before any trading.

- **Before trading:** the coin is fair (mean 3 heads) or always heads (6 heads) with equal odds, so the expected value is 4.5.
- **Always-heads coin:** an informed trader would value the contract at 6 and never sell at 3. Only a noise trader would sell, with probability about 0.65 × 0.19 ≈ 0.12.
- **Fair coin:** an informed trader sells when there are 2 or fewer heads (probability 22/64), giving 0.35 × 0.34 ≈ 0.12. A noise trader adds another 0.12, so the total is about 0.24.
- **Updated odds:** the chance the coin is always-heads falls to about 0.34.
- **Updated value:**
  - The always-heads case contributes 0.34 × 6 ≈ 2.0.
  - In the fair case, a sell suggests few heads, so the expected count is about 2.3. That contributes 0.66 × 2.3 ≈ 1.5.
  - The total is about 3.6.

I'm long one unit, so I'll set my quotes slightly below that estimate. I'll keep them fairly wide because informed traders are a big risk here.

{"bid": 2.6, "ask": 4.6}

Updating on the trading so far, I estimate fair value at about 4.06:

- **Starting value:** half the time the coin is fair, giving 3 heads on average. Half the time it always lands heads, giving 6. So the starting fair value is 4.5.
- **Quote 1 (they sold at 3):** an informed trader sells at 3 only if settlement is below 3. That shifts weight toward a fair coin with few heads, and the estimate falls to about 4.18.
- **Quote 2 (no trade at 2.6 / 4.6):** an informed trader stays out only if settlement is 3 or 4. That shifts weight toward those values, and the estimate falls to about 4.06.

The outcome is very uncertain: it is either exactly 6 or spread across 0 to 5, so I quote wide. I am already long one unit, so I shade both prices slightly lower to make selling a little more likely than buying.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 5.2}

I'm pricing this at about 5.6.

**Posterior on the coin after two heads**
- P(heads, heads | fair coin) = 0.25, so the fair branch has weight 0.5 × 0.25 = 0.125.
- P(heads, heads | double-headed coin) = 1, so that branch has weight 0.5 × 1 = 0.5.
- P(fair) = 0.125 / 0.625 = 0.2, and P(double-headed) = 0.8.

**Fair value**
- Each of the 4 remaining flips is heads with probability 0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.9.
- Expected settlement is 2 + 4 × 0.9 = 5.6.
- The settlement is 6 with probability 0.8 + 0.2/16 ≈ 0.81.
- The settlement can never be above 6.

**Ask at 6.0**
- An informed buyer only buys if the value is above 6, which cannot happen.
- Noise buyers will still sometimes buy at 6.0, and each of those trades is profitable or break-even.

**Bid at 4.9**
- This is about 0.7 below fair value, which protects me from informed sellers.
- Those sellers only exist on the fair-coin branch with a low count, about a 14% chance.
- Being long 1 is fine here.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.0}

The public fair value is about 5.6, and almost all of the risk is the true value being 6. So I quote a bid of 5.0 and an ask of 5.9.

**Which coin it is.** Two heads in a row is 4 times more likely with the always-heads coin (probability 1) than with the fair coin (0.25). Starting from 50/50, the chance it is the always-heads coin is now 0.8.

**Expected settlement.** Two heads are already counted.
- Always-heads coin: the 4 remaining flips add 4, for a total of 6.
- Fair coin: the 4 remaining flips add 2 on average, for a total of 4.
- Expected total: 2 + 0.8 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 = 5.6.

The value is exactly 6 with probability 0.8 + 0.2 × (1/16) ≈ 0.81.

**Ask at 5.9.** An informed trader buys at 5.9 almost only when the value is 6. That costs me just 0.1 per unit. Noise traders valuing above 5.9 still pay well above the 5.6 fair value.

**Bid at 5.0.** Informed traders sell at 5.0 only when the value is 4 or less. That happens when the coin is fair and shows at most 2 heads in the last 4 flips: 0.2 × 11/16 ≈ 0.14. Noise traders who sell below 5.0 give me a unit worth about 5.6 on average.

My position is +1, well inside the ±5 limit, so I can quote both sides.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 5.9}

Fair value is now about 5.3: two heads raised the chance of the always-heads coin, and the sale at 5 pulled it back down a little. With the bid at 4.6 and the ask at 5.8, the quote sits slightly below that because I'm long 2.

**Prior after two heads.** The coin always lands heads with probability 0.8 and is fair with probability 0.2.
- The four remaining flips are expected to give 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 3.6 heads.
- Adding the two heads already shown gives a fair value of 5.6.

**Update from the sale at 5 in quote 5.**
- If the coin always lands heads, the contract settles at 6, so an informed trader would never sell at 5. Only noise traders sell, with probability about 0.65 × 0.36 ≈ 0.23.
- If the coin is fair, an informed trader sells whenever the settlement is below 5. That happens with probability 11/16 ≈ 0.69. Total sell probability is about 0.35 × 0.69 + 0.23 ≈ 0.47.
- The odds become 0.8 × 0.23 : 0.2 × 0.47, so the coin always lands heads with probability about 0.66.
- If the coin is fair, the sale also suggests few heads to come, so I take its expected settlement as roughly 3.8.
- The fair value is about 0.66 × 6 + 0.34 × 3.8 ≈ 5.26.

**Quote.** I centre the quote around 5.2, set a fairly wide spread because the informed-trader risk is high, and shade it slightly lower because I'm long 2.

{"bid": 4.6, "ask": 5.8}

The coin must be fair, because flips 3 and 4 came up tails and a coin with P(heads) = 1 never shows tails.

**Fair value**
- Heads so far: 2.
- Flips 5 and 6 are each 50/50, so the settlement is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25.
- Fair value is 3.

**Quote choice**
- An informed counterparty only trades with me when the value is 2 (it sells at my bid) or 4 (it buys at my ask).
- Any ask between 3 and 4 is hit only by an informed trader holding value 4. A higher ask in that range loses less to them and earns more per noise trade.
- Noise traders have valuations around 3 with standard deviation 1.7, so a fairly wide spread still trades often enough to pay.
- I am long 2, so I set the quote slightly lower than symmetric. This makes selling a little more likely than buying.

{"bid": 2.1, "ask": 3.6}

Tails seen, so the coin is fair. Heads so far: 2. Remaining 2 flips are Binomial(2, 0.5), mean 1, giving fair value 3.

Possible settlement values: 2 (prob 0.25), 3 (prob 0.5), 4 (prob 0.25).

Quote 7 at 2.1 / 3.6 did not trade, which tells us little. The public fair value is 3.

An informed counterparty would sell at a bid of 2.5 only if the value is 2, and buy at an ask of 3.5 only if the value is 4. Noise traders' valuations are 3 plus noise with standard deviation 1.7, so quoting 2.5 / 3.5 captures about 0.5 of edge per noise trade. I am long 2, so I shade the quote slightly lower to lean towards selling.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 3.4}

The coin must be the fair one, because two tails have appeared. Two heads are already in, and flips 5 and 6 are fair. So settlement is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4, and fair value is 3.

**Informed traders:** if my bid and ask are at least 1 away from 3, an informed trader never trades. The worst case is a value of 2 or 4, and neither crosses a quote at 2 or below, or 4 or above. Inside that distance, I lose to them whenever the value is 2 or 4.

**Noise traders:** their valuation is 3 plus noise with standard deviation 1.7. If each quote is a distance h from 3, my expected profit from them is about 1.3 × h × P(noise > h).

| h | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | about 0.36 |
| 1.3 | about 0.375 |
| 1.5 | about 0.37 |

The best is around h = 1.3, which gives a bid of 1.7 and an ask of 4.3. My position of +1 is well within limits, so it doesn't change the quote.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

- Four flips remain.
- If the coin is always-heads, they add 4 heads.
- If it is fair, they add 2 heads on average.
- Expected remaining heads = 0.8 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 = 3.6.
- Expected total = 2 + 3.6 = 5.6.

**Last trade.** Someone bought at 6.0. The settlement can never exceed 6, so an informed trader would never pay 6. That buyer was a noise trader, and the trade tells me nothing about the coin.

**Ask at 6.0.** Informed traders can never buy here, so this side has no adverse selection. A noise trader still buys about 38% of the time.

**Bid at 4.9.** An informed trader only sells here if the coin is fair and the total ends at 4 or less. That happens with probability about 0.2 × 11/16 ≈ 0.14, which is an acceptable risk.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 6.0}

Two heads so far, so the posterior is P(always-heads coin) = 0.8 and P(fair coin) = 0.2.

**Fair value.** Expected settlement is 2 + 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = **5.6**. The distribution is lopsided: P(settle = 6) is about 0.81, and the rest is spread over 2 to 5.

**Ask.** Settlement can never exceed 6, so an informed trader never buys at an ask of 6.0. A noise trader with valuation above 6 still buys. At quote 4 someone bought at 6, which must have been a noise trader.

**Bid.** Informed traders sell only when settlement comes out below my bid. That only happens in the fair-coin outcomes, which have low probability. A bid near 4.8 limits that adverse selection while still buying from low noise valuations.

{"bid": 4.8, "ask": 6.0}

Four heads in a row strongly favour the biased coin. The fair-coin odds are 1/17, so P(biased) = 16/17. Expected heads in the last two flips is 33/17 ≈ 1.94, which puts fair value near **5.94**.

Settlement can only be 4, 5 or 6.
- **Ask:** An informed trader values the contract at most 6, so an ask above 6 is never hit by them. I estimated profit per quote as edge times the chance a noise trader crosses. That favours an ask around 7, giving about 1.06 edge at roughly a 21% fill chance.
- **Bid:** Setting the bid below 5 means an informed seller with value 5 won't hit it. At 4.9 the edge is about 1.04, with a fill chance of roughly 21% from noise traders.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 7.0}

Four heads in four flips makes the always-heads coin very likely.

**Fair value**
- Probability of four heads with the fair coin is 1/16. With the always-heads coin it is 1.
- So the posterior that the coin is always-heads is 16/17.
- Expected heads in flips 5 and 6 is 2 with the always-heads coin and 1 with the fair coin.
- Fair value = 4 + (16/17)·2 + (1/17)·1 = 4 + 33/17 ≈ 5.94.
- The settlement value is 6 with probability about 0.956. It is 5 or 4 with probability about 3/68 ≈ 0.044.

**Ask at 6.0**
- An informed trader values the contract at 6 at most, so it never buys at 6.0.
- A noise trader buys if its valuation is above 6.0, about 48% of the time. Each sale earns about 0.06.

**Bid at 5.2**
- A noise trader sells if its valuation is below 5.2, about 28% of the time. Each purchase gains about 0.74 against fair value.
- An informed trader sells only if the true value is 5 or 4, about 4.4% of the time. That costs about 0.2–1.2 per trade.
- Expected profit on the bid side is clearly positive.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 6.0}

With four heads in four flips, the coin is very likely the always-heads one. The settlement value is almost certainly 6.

**Posterior on the coin**
- Chance of four heads with the fair coin: ½ × (1/16) = 1/32.
- Chance of four heads with the always-heads coin: ½ × 1 = 1/2.
- So P(always-heads) = 16/17 and P(fair) = 1/17.

**Expected settlement value**
- If always-heads, flips 5 and 6 add 2 heads. If fair, they add 1 head on average.
- E = 4 + (16/17)·2 + (1/17)·1 ≈ 5.94.
- Settlement is 6 with about 96% probability, 5 with about 3%, and 4 with about 1.5%.

**Quote**
- **Ask at 6.0.** An informed trader values the contract at 6 or less, so it never buys at an ask of 6. Noise traders centred near 5.94 buy about half the time. That sale is roughly break-even or slightly positive.
- **Bid at 5.6.** Noise traders below that sell to me at a modest edge versus fair value. An informed trader only sells when settlement is 4 or 5, which is rare.

{"bid": 5.6, "ask": 6.0}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 1/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
A noise trader or an informed trader who knows the value is below 34 sold to me at 34, so I've revised my fair value down to about 37.

**Starting fair value.** Expected heads per flip is 0.4×0.3 + 0.1×0.4 + 0.5×0.9 = 0.61. The contract's starting fair value is therefore 10 × 8 × 0.61 = 48.8.

**Chance of a sale at 34 by trader type:**
- **Noise trader:** its valuation is 48.8 plus noise with standard deviation 26. The chance it falls below 34 is about 0.28. Weighted by 0.65, that gives about 0.185.
- **Informed trader:** it sells only if the true value is below 34, meaning 3 or fewer heads.
  - That happens about 81% of the time with the 0.3 coin, 59% with the 0.4 coin and almost never with the 0.9 coin.
  - Weighting by the coin probabilities gives about 0.38.
  - Weighted by 0.35, that gives about 0.134.

**Updated fair value.**
- If the seller was informed, the average value is about 20.
- Combining both cases: (0.185×48.8 + 0.134×20) / (0.185 + 0.134) ≈ 37.

**Quote.** I centre around 37 with a wide spread, because the value is spread between a low-coin outcome near 25 and a high-coin outcome near 72. I shade slightly lower because I'm already long one unit.

{"bid": 23, "ask": 49}

The fair value is about 22.9. I quote around it with a slight downward skew because I'm already long one unit.

**Which coin it probably is.** Flips 1–4 showed 1 head and 3 tails. Updating the prior on that result:

| Coin P(heads) | Prior | Chance of 1H 3T in that order | Prior × chance | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.4 | 0.1029 | 0.04116 | ≈ 0.819 |
| 0.4 | 0.1 | 0.0864 | 0.00864 | ≈ 0.172 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.0009 | 0.00045 | ≈ 0.009 |

The products sum to 0.05025, which gives the posteriors. The expected chance of heads on each remaining flip is now about 0.32.

**Fair value.** The one head already seen is worth 10. The 4 unrevealed flips add an expected 4 × 0.32 × 10 ≈ 12.9. That gives a fair value of about 22.9.

**Spread.** The settlement value still has a standard deviation of about 9 from the 4 remaining flips. Informed traders know the outcome, so I keep the spread fairly wide at about ±8. I shade both sides down by about 1 to lean against my long position.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 30}

Fair value ≈ 23: the revealed flips (1 head, 3 tails) put about 82% weight on the p = 0.3 coin, so about 1.3 more heads are expected in the last 4 flips. I quote around that, wide enough to cover informed traders.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 30}

The fair value is about 26.4, so I quote a bid of 22 and an ask of 31.

**Fair value.** Two heads in six flips makes the low-bias coins much more likely. Each coin's weight is its prior times the chance of this exact sequence, p²(1−p)⁴:

| Coin | Prior | p²(1−p)⁴ | Weighted | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P(heads) = 0.3 | 0.4 | 0.0216 | 0.00864 | ≈ 0.804 |
| P(heads) = 0.4 | 0.1 | 0.0207 | 0.00207 | ≈ 0.193 |
| P(heads) = 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.000081 | 0.00004 | ≈ 0.004 |

- The expected heads probability is about 0.322.
- Two flips remain, so the expected extra heads are 2 × 0.322 = 0.643.
- The fair value is 20 (the two heads so far × 10) + 6.4 = **about 26.4**.

**Possible settlements:** 20 (about 46%), 30 (about 44%) or 40 (about 10%).

**Choosing the quote.**
- With a bid of 22, an informed trader sells to me only when settlement is 20, and I lose 2.
- With an ask of 31, an informed trader buys from me only when settlement is 40, and I lose 9.
- In both cases the loss is small.
- Noise traders arrive around 26.4 with a spread of 26, so a quote about 4–5 points either side of fair value should catch them often.

{"bid": 22, "ask": 31}

Fair value is about 26.4 given 2 heads in 6 flips. That comes from a posterior of about 80% on p=0.3, 19% on p=0.4 and 0.4% on p=0.9, so E[p] is about 0.32.

The informed trader's possible settlement values are:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 20 | ≈0.46 |
| 30 | ≈0.43 |
| 40 | ≈0.10 |

Bid 21 and ask 32 earn a wide margin on noise traders on both sides, while keeping the loss to informed traders small.

{"bid": 21, "ask": 32}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The fair value is 24.8, so I quote 19.8 / 29.8, which is 5 either side.

- **Probability of heads:** the expected chance of heads is 0.6×0.5 + 0.4×0.8 = 0.62.
- **Fair value:** expected heads are 8 × 0.62 = 4.96, so the contract is worth 5 × 4.96 = 24.8.
- **Uncertainty:** the settlement value has a standard deviation of about 8.8. Informed traders therefore have a large edge, and the spread needs to be wide.
- **Choosing the half-spread:** I compared half-spreads of 4, 5 and 6 by expected gain from noise traders. All three come out at about 1.7–1.8. At 5, the expected loss to informed traders is only about 0.5, so 5 either side is a reasonable middle choice.

{"bid": 19.8, "ask": 29.8}

Posterior after two heads: P(0.8) ∝ 0.4·0.64 = 0.256 and P(0.5) ∝ 0.6·0.25 = 0.15. That gives P(0.8) ≈ 0.6305.

Expected probability of heads on the next flip ≈ 0.6305·0.8 + 0.3695·0.5 = 0.689.

Fair value = 5 × (2 + 6 × 0.689) = 5 × 6.134 ≈ 30.67.

The value can still move a lot over the remaining six flips, so I'll quote a wide spread of about ±3.5 around 30.7.

{"bid": 27.2, "ask": 34.2}

Fair value from public information:

- **Coin posterior after two heads:** The two heads have likelihood 0.25 under the fair coin and 0.64 under the biased coin. So P(biased) = 0.256 / 0.406 ≈ 0.63.
- **Heads probability for the remaining flips:** 0.5 × 0.37 + 0.8 × 0.63 ≈ 0.69.
- **Expected value:** Expected heads are 2 + 6 × 0.69 ≈ 6.14, so the contract is worth about 30.7.

The sale at my bid of 27.2 is mild evidence of a lower value, since an informed trader sells only if the value is below the bid. I shade fair value down to about 30.2.

I am already long 1, so I skew the quote slightly lower to make selling a bit more likely than buying.

{"bid": 26.6, "ask": 33.2}

Fair value is about 30.2, so I quote 26.7 / 32.9, skewed slightly down because I am long 1.

**Fair value from the reveals.** Flips 1 and 2 were both heads.
- The probability of two heads is 0.6 × 0.25 = 0.15 for the fair coin and 0.4 × 0.64 = 0.256 for the biased coin.
- So P(biased coin) = 0.256 / 0.406 ≈ 0.63.
- That gives P(heads) = 0.5 + 0.3 × 0.63 ≈ 0.69.

**Expected settlement.** Expected heads are 2 + 6 × 0.69 ≈ 6.13, so the contract is worth about 5 × 6.13 ≈ 30.7.

**Adjusting for trades.** Someone sold to me at 27.2, which may have been an informed seller, so I shade fair value down to about 30.2. The no-trade at 26.6 / 33.2 tells me little.

**Quote.** I keep the spread about as wide as before, since informed traders are a risk. My position is +1, so I lower both sides a little to make selling more likely than buying.

{"bid": 26.7, "ask": 32.9}

With 5 heads in the first 7 flips, the settlement value is either 25 (flip 8 tails) or 30 (flip 8 heads).

**Which coin is it?**
- How likely 5 heads in 7 flips is under each coin:
  - Fair coin: 0.5^7 = 0.0078.
  - Biased coin: 0.8^5 × 0.2^2 = 0.0131.
- Weighting by the prior chances of 3/5 and 2/5 gives a 0.528 chance that the coin is the biased one.

**Expected value**
- Chance flip 8 is heads: 0.472 × 0.5 + 0.528 × 0.8 = 0.658.
- Fair value: 25 + 5 × 0.658 ≈ 28.29.

**Quote**
- Bid 25.0: an informed trader who knows the value is 25 will not sell to me at 25. Noise traders who sell give me about 3.3 of edge.
- Ask 30.0: an informed trader who knows the value is 30 will not buy from me at 30. Noise traders who buy give me about 1.7 of edge.
- Quoting at exactly the two possible outcomes means the informed trader never trades profitably against me.
- Staying long by one unit is fine at these prices.

{"bid": 25.0, "ask": 30.0}

Five of the first seven flips are heads, so only flip 8 is still unknown.

**Which coin is it?**
- Chance of this sequence with the fair coin: 0.5⁷ ≈ 0.00781. Weighted by its 3/5 prior, that gives 0.00469.
- Chance with the biased coin: 0.8⁵ × 0.2² ≈ 0.01311. Weighted by its 2/5 prior, that gives 0.00524.
- So the chance the coin is biased is about 0.528.

**Fair value**
- Chance flip 8 is heads: 0.5 + 0.3 × 0.528 ≈ 0.658.
- Settlement is 25 if flip 8 is tails and 30 if heads.
- Expected settlement is 25 + 5 × 0.658 ≈ 28.3.

**Quote choice**
- An informed trader values the contract at exactly 25 or 30.
- With a bid of 25.0 and an ask of 30.0, an informed trader never trades, because its valuation is never strictly beyond my price.
- That removes adverse selection completely. Noise traders can still trade with me, and each such trade has positive expected edge around the fair value of 28.3.

{"bid": 25.0, "ask": 30.0}

Seven flips are revealed and 5 are heads, so the contract settles at either 25 (flip 8 tails) or 30 (flip 8 heads).

**Which coin is it?**
- If P(heads) = 0.5: the chance of these 7 flips is 0.5^7 ≈ 0.0078. Weighted by the prior 0.6, that gives 0.0047.
- If P(heads) = 0.8: the chance is 0.8^5 × 0.2^2 ≈ 0.0131. Weighted by the prior 0.4, that gives 0.0052.
- So the chance it is the 0.8 coin is about 0.529.

**Fair value**
- P(flip 8 is heads) = 0.471 × 0.5 + 0.529 × 0.8 ≈ 0.659.
- Fair value = 25 + 5 × 0.659 ≈ 28.29.

**Informed traders**
- If my bid is at most 25 and my ask is at least 30, an informed trader never trades with me.
- So I only need to price against noise traders, who value the contract at 28.29 plus noise with standard deviation 6.6.

**Ask: expected edge = (ask − 28.29) × P(valuation above ask)**

| Ask | Edge × chance | Expected edge |
|---|---|---|
| 31 | 2.71 × 0.34 | 0.92 |
| 32 | 3.71 × 0.29 | 1.07 |
| 33 | 4.71 × 0.24 | 1.12 |
| 34 | 5.71 × 0.19 | 1.11 |

The best ask is about 33.3.

**Bid: expected edge = (28.29 − bid) × P(valuation below bid)**

| Bid | Edge × chance | Expected edge |
|---|---|---|
| 25 | 3.29 × 0.31 | 1.02 |
| 24 | 4.29 × 0.26 | 1.11 |
| 23 | 5.29 × 0.21 | 1.12 |

The best bid is about 23.3.

{"bid": 23.3, "ask": 33.3}

info.raw:
Fair value is about 4.25, so I'm quoting 3.0 / 5.2.

1. **Coin after flip 1 = heads.** I weighted each coin's prior chance by how likely it is to show heads:
   - 0.2 coin: 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06
   - 0.5 coin: 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.20
   - 0.7 coin: 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.21
   - These sum to 0.47, giving updated chances of about 0.128, 0.426 and 0.447.

2. **Expected chance of heads per remaining flip.** Weighting each coin's heads chance by these gives about 0.551.

3. **Expected heads in total.** Six flips remain, so expected future heads are 6 × 0.551 ≈ 3.31. Adding the known head gives about 4.31.

4. **Trading history.** Someone sold to me at 2.3 in stage 1. That is weak evidence the value is lower, so I shade fair value to about 4.25.

5. **Quote width and skew.** The spread is about ±1.1 around fair value, to cover the 20% chance of an informed counterparty. I shift both sides down slightly because I am already long one unit, which makes selling a bit more likely than buying.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.2}

After flip 1 came up heads, the posterior over the coin bias is about 0.128 for 0.2, 0.426 for 0.5 and 0.447 for 0.7.

That gives an expected bias of about 0.551. The fair value is 1 + 6 × 0.551 ≈ 4.31.

The last counterparty bought at 5.2, which points slightly upward. I'll centre the quote a little above 4.3 and keep it wide to protect against informed traders.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 5.3}

Fair value after flip 1 = heads is about **4.3**, so I'll quote 3.4 / 5.2 around it.

**Updating the coin's bias on the head.** Each coin's weight is its prior probability times its chance of heads:
- p = 0.2: 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06
- p = 0.5: 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.20
- p = 0.7: 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.21

The weights sum to 0.47. The expected bias is (0.012 + 0.100 + 0.147) / 0.47 ≈ 0.551.

**Fair value of the contract.** One head is already counted, and 6 flips remain. Expected heads = 1 + 6 × 0.551 ≈ 4.31.

**Reading the trade history.** In this stage, one counterparty sold to me at 3.5 and one bought from me at 5.2. One trade on each side roughly cancels out, so I keep my estimate at about 4.3.

**Inventory.** I'm long 1 unit, so I set the bid slightly further from fair value than the ask.

{"bid": 3.4, "ask": 5.2}

Expected settlement is about 4.2 heads, and I'm quoting a 3.2 bid and 4.8 ask around a centre of about 4.0.

**Coin posterior after flips 1, 1, 0 (two heads, one tail):**

| P(heads) | Prior | Likelihood p²(1−p) | Weight | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.3 | 0.032 | 0.0096 | 0.093 |
| 0.5 | 0.4 | 0.125 | 0.0500 | 0.482 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 | 0.147 | 0.0441 | 0.425 |

The weights sum to 0.1037. The posterior mean of P(heads) is about 0.557.

**Fair value:**
- Four flips remain, so I expect 4 × 0.557 ≈ 2.23 more heads.
- With 2 heads already seen, the fair value is about 4.23.
- Counterparties sold to me at my bid twice in stage 2. That hints slightly that the true value is lower, so I shade fair value to about 4.1.

**Position skew:** I am long 2 units, close to the +3 limit. I lower my centre to about 4.0 so that selling is more likely than buying.

**Quote:** I keep a spread of about 1.6. This guards against informed traders while still trading with noise traders, whose valuations have a standard deviation of 2.7.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 4.8}

Fair value is about 4.2, set by the revealed flips (H, H, T) and the coin posterior.

**Posterior on the coin.** The likelihood of H, H, T is p²(1−p). Multiplying by each prior:
- p = 0.2: 0.3 × 0.032 = 0.0096
- p = 0.5: 0.4 × 0.125 = 0.050
- p = 0.7: 0.3 × 0.147 = 0.0441

These sum to 0.1037. Normalised, the weights are about 0.09, 0.48 and 0.43.

**Fair value.** E[p] ≈ 0.557. Four flips remain, so expected remaining heads ≈ 4 × 0.557 = 2.23. Adding the 2 heads already shown gives a fair value of about 4.23.

**Quote.** The trade history doesn't point one way: in stage 2 people both bought and sold, and the last trade was a buy. I'm long 1, so I skew my quotes slightly down to make selling a bit more likely. I'll quote about 1 either side of fair.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 5.0}

Fair value is about 4.2:

- **Posterior on the coin.** Flips 1–3 (heads, heads, tails) give these probabilities for the coin's P(heads):
  - 0.2: about 0.09
  - 0.5: about 0.48
  - 0.7: about 0.43
- **Expected heads per remaining flip.** This works out to about 0.557.
- **Fair value.** There are 4 unrevealed flips, so fair value is 2 (heads so far) + 4 × 0.557 ≈ 4.23.

The two stage-3 trades so far (one buy, one sell) roughly cancel, so they don't move the estimate. I'm long 2, so I shade both prices down slightly to encourage selling. I keep the spread wide enough to guard against informed traders.

{"bid": 3.3, "ask": 4.8}

Fair value is about 4.15. After flips 1–5 (3 heads, 2 tails), the posterior on the coin is:
- P(p=0.2) ≈ 0.07
- P(p=0.5) ≈ 0.54
- P(p=0.7) ≈ 0.40

That gives E[p] ≈ 0.56. Two flips remain, so the expected settlement is 3 + 2 × 0.56 ≈ 4.12. The last counterparty bought at 4.5, which nudges this up slightly, to about 4.15.

The settlement can only be 3, 4 or 5.
- **Ask:** An ask below 5 loses to an informed buyer only when the value is 5. I am long 2, so selling suits me, and I lean the ask slightly lower to 4.7.
- **Bid:** A bid of 3.5 loses to an informed seller only when the value is 3, so I keep it there.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 4.7}

Fair value is about 4.12: the 3 heads already revealed plus about 1.12 expected heads from the last two flips.

**Which coin is it?** After 3 heads and 2 tails, I weigh each coin by its prior times the chance of that result, p³(1−p)²:
- p = 0.2: 0.3 × 0.00512 = 0.00154
- p = 0.5: 0.4 × 0.03125 = 0.01250
- p = 0.7: 0.3 × 0.03087 = 0.00926

Normalising gives weights of about 0.066, 0.537 and 0.397.

**Expected heads still to come:** The expected bias is about 0.066 × 0.2 + 0.537 × 0.5 + 0.397 × 0.7 ≈ 0.56. Over the two hidden flips that is about 1.12 expected heads, which gives the 4.12 total.

**Quote:** The settlement value will almost certainly be 3, 4 or 5, so I quote a fairly wide spread around 4.12. I am long 2, so I shade both prices down slightly to favour selling over buying.

{"bid": 3.4, "ask": 4.6}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 2.58 heads. The average heads probability is 0.43, and 6 × 0.43 = 2.58.

- **What informed traders know:** they know the exact settlement, which is a whole number. They buy at my ask only when the true count is 3 or more, and sell at my bid only when it is 2 or less.
- **How uncertain the settlement is:** its standard deviation is about 1.3. Noise traders' valuations spread by a similar 1.3 around fair value.
- **Choosing the quote:** I keep the quote fairly wide around 2.58 so the spread covers losses to informed traders. I narrow it slightly from last time because the 1.8/3.4 quote drew no trade.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 3.2}

Flip 1 came up heads, so I updated the coin probabilities on that result:
- The weights before normalising are 0.2·0.3 = 0.06, 0.3·0.4 = 0.12 and 0.5·0.5 = 0.25.
- After normalising, the expected P(heads) is about 0.444.

Fair value is the 1 head already seen plus the expected heads in the remaining 5 flips: 1 + 5·0.444 ≈ 3.22. The uncertainty in those 5 flips is about 1.1, and half of counterparties know the exact value. So I'm quoting roughly 1 point either side of fair value. I'm skewing the quote slightly lower because I'm already long 1.

{"bid": 2.2, "ask": 4.1}

Fair value from public information is about 3.2: after flip 1 came up heads, the expected chance of heads is about 0.444, so 1 + 5 × 0.444 ≈ 3.2.

The sell at my bid of 2.2 points lower. A noise trader would only sell that low about 22% of the time. An informed trader would sell if the total ends up at 2 or less, which is roughly 25% likely. So the trade is real evidence of a low value, and I shade my estimate down to about 2.9.

I'm already long 2, so I quote a slightly lower bid and an ask that is close enough to get lifted.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 3.4}

Two heads have shown in five flips, so the settlement will be either 2 or 3. That depends only on flip 6.

**Posterior on the coin's heads probability, given 2 heads in 5 flips:**
- p = 0.3: 0.2 × 0.3² × 0.7³ ≈ 0.00617
- p = 0.4: 0.3 × 0.4² × 0.6³ ≈ 0.01037
- p = 0.5: 0.5 × 0.5⁵ ≈ 0.01563

So E[p] ≈ 0.429, and the fair value is about 2 + 0.429 = **2.43**.

**Quote choice:**
- An informed trader values the contract at exactly 2 or exactly 3. It trades only if the ask is strictly below 3 or the bid is strictly above 2.
- Quoting a bid of 1.9 and an ask of 3.0 means informed traders never trade with me.
- Noise traders value it at 2.43 plus noise with standard deviation 1.3. About a third of them sell at 1.9, which earns me roughly 0.53 per trade.
- About a third of them buy at 3.0, which earns me roughly 0.57 per trade.
- I am long 2, so a sale also reduces my position.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 3.0}

Five flips are revealed, with 2 heads. The only remaining uncertainty is flip 6, so the contract settles at either 2 or 3.

**Posterior on the coin's bias**, given 2 heads in 5 flips, weighting each prior by p²(1−p)³:

| P(heads) | Prior × likelihood | Share |
|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.2 × 0.03087 = 0.00617 | ≈19% |
| 0.4 | 0.3 × 0.03456 = 0.01037 | ≈32% |
| 0.5 | 0.5 × 0.03125 = 0.01563 | ≈49% |

This gives E[p] ≈ 0.429, so fair value ≈ 2 + 0.43 = 2.43.

**Quote choice:**
- **Bid 2.0:** An informed trader knows the value is 2 or 3. A trader who knows 2 only sells if the bid is above 2, so at 2.0 no informed trader sells to me. Only noise traders hit it, and each such trade gains about 0.43 in expectation. Buying one more unit takes me to +4, which is within the limit.
- **Ask 3.0:** A trader who knows 3 only buys if the ask is below 3, so at 3.0 no informed trader lifts it. Only noise traders do, and each such trade gains about 0.57 in expectation.

Both sides are protected from informed traders and earn a positive expected profit from noise traders.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The fair value is 43.4, and I'm quoting about 8 points either side of it: bid 35.4, ask 51.4.

**Fair value**
- The expected chance of heads is 0.4×0.5 + 0.6×0.7 = 0.62.
- Over 7 flips that gives 0.62 × 7 = 4.34 expected heads, so the contract is worth 43.4.

**How uncertain the settlement is**
- The variance of the number of heads is 0.4×1.75 + 0.6×1.47 + 0.47 ≈ 2.05.
  - The first two terms are the average variance of 7 flips for each coin.
  - The 0.47 term comes from not knowing which coin it is.
- That is a standard deviation of about 1.43 heads, or about 14 in contract value.

**Spread**
- Informed traders (35% of counterparties) know the exact settlement, which could be as much as 14 or more away from fair value. Trading with them is costly.
- Noise traders' valuations are spread with a standard deviation of 11. Quoting about 8 points from fair value still trades with a fair share of them while limiting losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 35.4, "ask": 51.4}

Fair value is about 45.1 after the reveal, so I quote 40 / 51 around it.

- **Fair value:** The likelihood of tails, heads, heads is 0.125 for the fair coin and 0.147 for the 0.7 coin. With the 2/5 and 3/5 prior, the chance it is the 0.7 coin is 0.0882 / 0.1382 ≈ 0.64. That gives P(heads) ≈ 0.628, so the 4 remaining flips should add about 2.51 heads. Adding the 2 heads already shown gives about 4.51 heads, or about 45.1.
- **Earlier trade:** Someone bought from me at 50.4 in stage 1. That hints at a higher value, but it was before the reveal, so I give it little weight.
- **Spread:** The remaining flips leave about ±10 of uncertainty in the settlement value. Informed traders will mostly hold whole values like 40, 50 or 60, so I keep the spread wide.
- **Position:** I am short 1, so I set the quote slightly above fair value, closer to the ask.

{"bid": 40.0, "ask": 51.0}

Fair value from public information is about 45.1, though the two buys at my ask hint at upside.

**Posterior on the coin after flips 0, 1, 1:**
- Likelihood of this sequence if P(heads) = 0.5: 0.125. Times prior 2/5 gives 0.05.
- Likelihood if P(heads) = 0.7: 0.3 × 0.7² = 0.147. Times prior 3/5 gives 0.0882.
- So P(coin is 0.7) = 0.0882 / 0.1382 ≈ 0.64.

**Expected settlement:**
- Expected heads per flip = 0.36 × 0.5 + 0.64 × 0.7 ≈ 0.63.
- Expected heads in the 4 remaining flips ≈ 2.51.
- Expected total ≈ 2 + 2.51 = 4.51 heads, so fair value ≈ 45.1.

**Quote:**
- I'm short 2, so I skew my quotes slightly upward.
- I keep the spread wide to protect against informed traders.
- The settlement value moves in steps of 10, so an ask of 52 is only hit by informed traders when the value is 60 or more.

{"bid": 40.5, "ask": 52}

The fair value is about 49.3, so I'll quote 45.0 / 54.0, roughly symmetric around it.

**Which coin it is.** The four revealed flips show 3 heads and 1 tail.
- The chance of seeing that result with the 0.5 coin, times its 2/5 prior, is 0.4 × 0.0625 = 0.0250.
- The same calculation for the 0.7 coin, with its 3/5 prior, is 0.6 × 0.1029 = 0.0617.
- So the probability that the coin is the 0.7 coin is about 0.71.

**Fair value.**
- The expected chance of heads on each remaining flip is 0.29 × 0.5 + 0.71 × 0.7 ≈ 0.642.
- Three flips are still unknown, so expected total heads are 3 + 3 × 0.642 ≈ 4.93.
- That gives a fair value of about 49.3.

**Quote.** The final value can only be 30, 40, 50 or 60, and an informed trader will pick me off at any price inside that range. A spread of about ±4.5 around fair value balances that risk against earning from noise traders. I'm short 2, which allows only a slight upward lean.

{"bid": 45.0, "ask": 54.0}

Fair value is about 49.3 from the revealed flips, nudged up slightly by the recent buys. Since I'm short 3, I'm quoting around 49.5 and skewing slightly up.

**Which coin it is.** The revealed flips are 0, 1, 1, 1, so 3 heads in 4 flips.
- Fair coin (P(heads) = 0.5): 0.4 × 0.5⁴ = 0.025
- Biased coin (P(heads) = 0.7): 0.6 × 0.7³ × 0.3 = 0.0617
- So P(biased coin) = 0.0617 / (0.025 + 0.0617) ≈ 0.71.

**Expected heads per remaining flip.** E[P(heads)] = 0.5 × 0.29 + 0.7 × 0.71 ≈ 0.642.

**Fair value.** The 3 heads seen so far are worth 30. The 3 remaining flips add about 3 × 0.642 × 10 ≈ 19.3. Fair value from flips alone is about 49.3.

**Adjustments.** Counterparties bought at my ask three times, which hints that the settlement value is higher. Being short 3 is also a reason to skew my quotes up. I'll centre the quote around 49.5 and keep the spread wide to guard against informed traders.

{"bid": 44, "ask": 55}

Fair value is about **56.7**, and I'm quoting a bid of 50 and an ask of 64.

**Fair value**
- The revealed flips show 5 heads in 6.
- Likelihood under a 0.5 coin: 0.4 × 0.5⁶ ≈ 0.00625.
- Likelihood under a 0.7 coin: 0.6 × 0.7⁵ × 0.3 ≈ 0.03025.
- So the posterior probability of the 0.7 coin is about 0.83.
- P(flip 7 is heads) = 0.17 × 0.5 + 0.83 × 0.7 ≈ 0.666.
- Settlement is 60 if flip 7 is heads and 50 if not, so fair value ≈ 56.66.

**Quotes**
- **Bid at 50:** an informed trader never sells to me at this price, since the value is at least 50. Expected profit from noise sellers is about 1.2 per quote.
- **Ask at 64:** this is above the highest possible value of 60, so informed traders never buy. Expected profit from noise buyers is about 1.2 per quote.

{"bid": 50, "ask": 64}

**Fair value.** Five of the six revealed flips are heads, so the coin is probably the 0.7 coin.

- Likelihood of the flips under the 0.5 coin: 0.5⁶ ≈ 0.0156.
- Likelihood under the 0.7 coin: 0.7⁵ × 0.3 ≈ 0.0504.
- Posterior probability of the 0.7 coin: (0.6 × 0.0504) / (0.4 × 0.0156 + 0.6 × 0.0504) ≈ 0.83.
- Probability flip 7 is heads: 0.17 × 0.5 + 0.83 × 0.7 ≈ 0.666.
- Five heads are already counted, so settlement is 50 or 60, and the fair value is about 56.7.

**Ask.**
- An informed trader with value 60 buys at any ask below 60, and I lose on that trade. So the ask should be at least 60.
- Above 60, only noise traders buy. Expected profit is (ask − 56.7) × P(noise valuation > ask).
- With noise standard deviation 11, this peaks about 8.3 above fair value, so I ask about 65.

**Bid.**
- An informed trader with value 50 sells at any bid above 50, so the bid should be at most 50.
- At or below 50, only noise traders sell.
- A bid of 50 gives about 6.7 × 0.27 ≈ 1.8 expected profit, and 48.4 gives about 1.9. The curve is flat here, so I bid 49.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The expected number of heads per flip is 0.6×0.4 + 0.4×0.8 = 0.56. Over 6 flips, the public fair value is 6 × 0.56 = 3.36.

The settlement value is spread out. With the p=0.4 coin, heads average 2.4. With the p=0.8 coin, heads average 4.8. So informed traders gain a lot when the value is far from 3.36. Noise traders have a standard deviation of 1.6, so a spread of about ±1.2 still catches a fair number of them while protecting against informed trades.

I'll quote a bid of 2.2 and an ask of 4.5.

{"bid": 2.2, "ask": 4.5}

The prior expected number of heads is 6 × (0.6×0.4 + 0.4×0.8) = 3.36. The counterparty selling to me at 2.2 nudges the fair value down a little, to about 3.2. I'm long 1, so I'll shade my quotes slightly lower to make a sale more likely than another buy.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 4.2}

Flip 1 came up heads, so the 0.8 coin is now more likely:

- P(coin is 0.8 | flip 1 = 1) = (0.4·0.8) / (0.4·0.8 + 0.6·0.4) = 0.32 / 0.56 = 4/7.
- Expected P(heads) is 4/7 · 0.8 + 3/7 · 0.4 ≈ 0.629.
- Expected settlement is 1 (flip 1) + 5 · 0.629 ≈ 4.14.

The sell to me at 2.2 in quote 1 is mild evidence of a lower value, because an informed trader might have sold. So I shade fair value down to about 4.0.

I set the spread wide enough to limit losses to informed traders while still catching noise trades. I lean the quotes slightly lower because I am already long one unit.

{"bid": 3.1, "ask": 4.9}

Fair value is about 4.3, so I quote 3.4 bid and 5.2 ask, roughly 0.9 either side, with my position at 0.

1. **Coin after flip 1 = heads.** P(0.8-coin) = (0.4 × 0.8) / (0.4 × 0.8 + 0.6 × 0.4) = 0.32 / 0.56 ≈ 0.571.
2. **Expected heads.** The expected heads-probability per remaining flip is 0.571 × 0.8 + 0.429 × 0.4 ≈ 0.629. Over the 5 remaining flips that gives about 3.14, plus the 1 known head, for a fair value of about 4.14.
3. **Trade history.** At quote 3 a counterparty bought at 4.9. That leans toward an informed trader seeing a value of 5 or more. I shift fair value up slightly, to about 4.3. This is a rough adjustment rather than an exact Bayesian update.
4. **Spread.** The 0.9 width on each side protects against the 20% chance the counterparty is informed. It still catches noise traders, whose valuations have a standard deviation of 1.6.

{"bid": 3.4, "ask": 5.2}

Three of the four revealed flips are heads, which favours the 0.8 coin.

**Which coin**
- Chance of seeing these flips with the 0.8 coin, times its prior: 0.4 × 0.8³ × 0.2 = 0.04096.
- The same for the 0.4 coin: 0.6 × 0.4³ × 0.6 = 0.02304.
- So P(0.8 coin) = 0.04096 / 0.064 = 0.64.

**Fair value**
- Chance each remaining flip is heads: 0.64 × 0.8 + 0.36 × 0.4 = 0.656.
- Two flips are left, so expected further heads = 2 × 0.656 ≈ 1.31.
- Fair value = 3 + 1.31 ≈ 4.31.

**Quote**
- Settlement can only be 3, 4 or 5, so an informed trader is most costly near those levels.
- I quote fairly wide around 4.31: bid 3.6, ask 4.9.
- I'm long 1, so I set the quote slightly low, which makes it a bit more likely I sell than buy.

{"bid": 3.6, "ask": 4.9}

Fair value is about 4.31. Three heads in four flips push the probability of the 0.8 coin to 0.64, so P(heads) on the next flip is about 0.656. That gives 3 + 2 × 0.656 ≈ 4.31.

The settlement value can only be 3, 4 or 5:

| Settlement | Flips 5 and 6 | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | two tails | about 0.155 |
| 4 | one head, one tail | about 0.378 |
| 5 | two heads | about 0.467 |

- **Ask at 5.0:** An informed buyer only trades if its value is strictly above my ask, so 5.0 can't lose to one. Noise traders above 5.0 still pay a good margin over 4.31.
- **Bid at 3.6:** I only lose to an informed seller when the value is 3, which costs 0.6. That needs both an informed trader (0.2) and two tails (about 0.155), so the expected cost is small. The bid still catches noise sellers about 0.7 below fair value.

Last quote got no trade, which tells us little. I keep a spread of about 9 points around fair value to guard against informed traders.

{"bid": 4.8, "ask": 13.9}

After two tails, the coin is most likely the low-heads one.

**Updating on the two tails.** The chance of two tails is 0.64 for the 0.2 coin, 0.09 for the 0.7 coin and 0.01 for the 0.9 coin. Weighting by the priors gives posteriors of 0.80, 0.169 and 0.031.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 8.0}

Fair value is about 4.4, so I'll quote roughly 3 points either side of it.

**Updating on the coin after two tails.** The prior weight of each coin times the chance of two tails:
- P = 0.2 coin: 0.2 × 0.64 = 0.128
- P = 0.7 coin: 0.3 × 0.09 = 0.027
- P = 0.9 coin: 0.5 × 0.01 = 0.005

These sum to 0.16. The updated chances are about 0.80, 0.17 and 0.03.

**Expected value.**
- The expected chance of heads is 0.80 × 0.2 + 0.17 × 0.7 + 0.03 × 0.9, which is about 0.306.
- Three flips remain, and each head is worth 5.
- So the expected settlement is 3 × 0.306 × 5, about 4.6.

**Adjusting for trading.** At quote 5, someone sold to me at 1.5. That is weak evidence the true value is lower, so I shade fair value down to about 4.4.

**Settlement values.** The contract can only settle at 0, 5, 10 or 15. My position is flat, so I can quote both sides.

{"bid": 1.4, "ask": 7.6}

Fair value is about 13.1. I quoted around it with a modest spread.

**Posterior on the coin after 2 heads and 2 tails.** The likelihood of this pattern is p²(1−p)².
- P(heads) = 0.2: 0.2 × 0.0256 = 0.00512, so posterior ≈ 0.229
- P(heads) = 0.7: 0.3 × 0.0441 = 0.01323, so posterior ≈ 0.591
- P(heads) = 0.9: 0.5 × 0.0081 = 0.00405, so posterior ≈ 0.181

The expected chance that flip 5 is heads is about 0.622.

**Fair value.** Settlement is 10 (flip 5 tails) or 15 (flip 5 heads). So fair value is 10 + 5 × 0.622 ≈ 13.1.

**Quote.**
- An informed counterparty sells to me only when settlement is 10, losing me (bid − 10) per trade. It buys from me only when settlement is 15, losing me (15 − ask).
- Noise traders are spread widely (standard deviation 12), so a moderate spread still gets trades.
- My position is +1, well inside the ±3 limit, so I quote both sides roughly symmetrically around 13.1.

{"bid": 11.8, "ask": 14.4}

The posterior fair value is about 13.1, so I'll quote roughly 1.5 either side of it, at 11.6 / 14.6.

**Posterior on the coin after flips 0, 0, 1, 1.** Each prior is weighted by the chance of seeing those four flips:
- P(heads) = 0.2: 0.2 × (0.8² × 0.2²) = 0.00512
- P(heads) = 0.7: 0.3 × (0.3² × 0.7²) = 0.01323
- P(heads) = 0.9: 0.5 × (0.1² × 0.9²) = 0.00405

These sum to 0.0224.

**Chance that flip 5 is heads.**
P = (0.00512 × 0.2 + 0.01323 × 0.7 + 0.00405 × 0.9) / 0.0224 ≈ 0.622

**Fair value.** Two heads are already revealed, worth 10. The contract therefore settles at 10 or 15, and its fair value is 10 + 5 × 0.622 ≈ 13.1.

**Quote.** Noise traders' valuations are centred on 13.1 with standard deviation 12, so a modest spread around fair value will catch many of them. An informed trader takes the bid only when settlement is 10 and lifts the ask only when it is 15. Quoting 1.5 either side of fair value keeps that informed loss limited. My position is +2, so I can still buy one more unit without breaching +3.
